context.in_practice: Route 1: the tool records the hand edit and saves that record on its own before it runs the command. If the command then fails, the record of the hand edit is still there. Only the failed command's own changes are missing. This matches how imports are recorded. Someone reading the history later sees the hand edit even if nothing else succeeded. Route 2: nobody decided this case. What happens follows from however the save happens to work. If the hand-edit record is saved together with the command, a failed command probably takes the record with it. The edit would then either be noticed again on the next run or never show up in the history. Users can't predict which, and maintainers have no stated rule to rely on.
context.stakes: When the tool notices that someone edited its files by hand, it records that edit. The question is whether that record survives when the command that noticed it then fails. If it doesn't survive, the history may not show a change that really happened.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 adds a separate save step, so a failed command can still leave a new entry in the history. Route 2 costs nothing up front, but whether a hand edit stays on record after a failure is left to chance.

plan_why: This question can't be shown with these commands. Reconcile only produces events when a file changes by hand after the theatre has been imported, and the first troupe command is what imports it. The listed files are created only once, before that first command, and every later command is `troupe` itself. No hand edit can happen between commands, so no command can reach a reconcile that has something to record, whether the command then fails or not. Pre-seeding state in .troupe/ would not help, because each implementation stores its event state in its own format.
routes: Yes; saved in their own save before the command body
